answer:
The best chain is QB7-QB12-QB11. QB12 is the middle qubit.

How I chose it: I read the current default calibration of the real Garnet chip. It is calibration set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade, with quality metrics from 2026-10-21 16:42Z. The set lists 28 CZ pairs, and each pair has an interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) fidelity. I checked every pair of CZ pairs that share one qubit.
- The QB12-QB7 CZ has fidelity 0.99802.
- The QB12-QB11 CZ has fidelity 0.99869.
- Their product is 0.99671. This is the highest of all chains.
- The runner-up is QB12-QB11-QB16, at 0.99469.

What I ran: a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB7, QB12 and QB11 on garnet:mock, with 200 shots. QB12 was put into an equal superposition. A CZ on QB12-QB7 with single-qubit rotations around it copied QB12's state onto QB7. A CZ on QB12-QB11 did the same for QB11. No other two-qubit gates were used. All 3 qubits were measured. I simulated the exact circuit on my computer first. It gives 000 half the time and 111 half the time, which is the ideal GHZ result.

Counts, in the order QB7 QB12 QB11: 000 = 52, 001 = 51, 110 = 47, 111 = 50. Job ID 01a16042-c937-7279-baee-5b9731bffeb4.

What the numbers mean: garnet:mock is a test target. It checks that the circuit is valid for the chip and then returns random bitstrings. It does not run the circuit on real qubits. So the counts do not show the GHZ pattern. A real QPU should mostly give 000 and 111. The principle is entanglement. In a GHZ state the three qubits are each random, but they always agree with each other. Picking the pairs with the best CZ fidelity keeps the most of that agreement on real hardware. The mock job cost 0 credits.
